propositions.text: The Applicant is a Jamaican citizen who lived and worked in Canada for many years and seeks judicial review of a PRRA refusal.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a citizen of Jamaica, who has lived and worked in Canada for many years. He seeks judicial review of a decision refusing his Pre-Removal Risk Assessment [PRRA] application.

propositions.text: The PRRA officer found the risk to the Applicant in Jamaica as an older, disabled returnee did not warrant refugee protection under IRPA ss.96 and 97.
propositions.quote: The PRRA officer [the Officer] determined that the risk the Applicant faced in Jamaica, as an older, disabled returnee, did not warrant refugee protection in Canada under s.96 and s.97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act [IRPA].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is a Jamaican citizen seeking judicial review of a PRRA refusal, where the Officer found no refugee protection warranted.

propositions.text: The application should be dismissed despite sympathy for the Applicant's situation.
propositions.quote: While I sympathize with the Applicant’s situation, I believe this application should be dismissed.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Officer to conclude no serious possibility of persecution or personalized risk of torture, life risk, or cruel punishment existed.
propositions.quote: It was reasonable for the Officer to conclude that the Applicant would not face mistreatment upon return to Jamaica amounting to either a) a serious possibility of persecution, or b) a personalized risk of torture, risk to life, or risk of cruel and unusual punishment.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Officer to find the Applicant failed to rebut the presumption of state protection.
propositions.quote: It was also reasonable for the Officer to conclude that the Applicant had failed to rebut the presumption of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer reasonably concluded no serious persecution or personalized risk and that the Applicant failed to rebut state protection presumption.

propositions.text: The Applicant is a 55-year-old Jamaican who worked as a Temporary Foreign Worker in Canada for about 25 years.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Linton Smith, is a 55-year-old Jamaican national who has spent the better part of the last 25 years as a Temporary Foreign Worker in Canada.

propositions.text: Mr. Smith first came to Canada in 1996 on a work permit and worked six weeks, continuing temporary work until April 2017.
propositions.quote: Mr. Smith first came to Canada in 1996 on a work permit and worked for six weeks. He continued in this pattern of temporary work, until he last entered Canada in April 2017.

propositions.text: The Applicant filed a first H&C application in 2017 and believed he retained status during its consideration, but status expired in 2018.
propositions.quote: The Applicant filed a first application for Permanent Residence based on Humanitarian and Compassionate Considerations [H&C] in 2017, and alleges he was under the impression that he retained his immigration status while the H&C application was being considered. However, the Applicant’s status expired in 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant's background: 55 years old, Jamaican, worked in Canada as Temporary Foreign Worker since 1996, filed H&C in 2017, status expired 2018.

propositions.text: In May 2019, the Applicant suffered a stroke causing physical impairments and was fired from his job and removed from his bunkhouse.
propositions.quote: In May 2019, the Applicant suffered a stroke that left him with physical impairments. Immediately after his stroke and hospitalization, he was fired from his job. This also resulted in his removal from the bunkhouse where he was living, as part of his employment.

propositions.text: His H&C application was refused after these events.
propositions.quote: His H&C application was subsequently refused.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant had a stroke in 2019, was fired and evicted, and his H&C application was refused.

propositions.text: After stroke and job loss, Applicant lost medical insurance and healthcare, impairing motor functions and speech.
propositions.quote: Mr. Smith testifies that after his stroke and his termination from work, his medical insurance was cancelled and he was left without healthcare. He was unable to follow the recommended rehabilitation treatments and as a result, he has impaired motor functions, particularly in the use of his hands, and he has impaired speech.

propositions.text: Applicant has no spouse or children and only siblings as immediate family in Jamaica.
propositions.quote: He has no spouse or children and no immediate family in Jamaica, other than siblings.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant lost healthcare after stroke, has motor and speech impairments, and only siblings as family in Jamaica.

propositions.text: The Applicant made a second H&C application, refused in February 2021.
propositions.quote: The Applicant made a second H&C application, which was also refused in February 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant's second H&C application was refused in February 2021.

propositions.text: Applicant was arrested by CBSA in December 2021 while reporting a crime and was offered a PRRA in May 2022.
propositions.quote: Mr. Smith was arrested by CBSA in December 2021, while attempting to report a crime to the OPP branch in Leamington. He was offered a PRRA in May 2022.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant was arrested by CBSA in December 2021 and offered a PRRA in May 2022.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted a third H&C application in September 2022, still undetermined, and was directed to report for removal in January 2023.
propositions.quote: In September 2022, the Applicant submitted his third H&C application, which has yet to be determined. The Applicant received a Direction to Report for his removal in January 2023;

propositions.text: Applicant filed a motion to stay removal in February 2023, which was granted.
propositions.quote: he filed a motion to stay his removal in February 2023, which was granted.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant filed a third H&C application in 2022, was directed to report for removal in 2023, and obtained a stay of removal.

propositions.text: Applicant alleges personalized risk of harm in Jamaica due to age, disability, returnee status, and workforce reentry.
propositions.quote: In the Applicant’s PRRA application, he alleged that he faces a personalized risk of harm in Jamaica due to his profile as an older person with a disability, seeking to rejoin the workforce, and as a returnee from overseas after several years living in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant alleges personalized risk of harm in Jamaica due to age, disability, and returnee status.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer refused the application, finding country conditions general and not specifically targeting the Applicant.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s PRRA was refused in a letter dated January 4, 2023. The Officer determined that while country conditions in Jamaica were not perfect, these conditions were general and applied to all residents, not to the Applicant particularly.

propositions.text: There was insufficient evidence that the Applicant would be singled out for different treatment based on personal circumstances.
propositions.quote: The Officer concluded that there was insufficient evidence to conclude that the Applicant would be singled out for treatment substantially different from other residents, based on his personal circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer refused the PRRA, finding country conditions general and no evidence Applicant would be singled out.

propositions.text: The Officer found societal discrimination against disabled persons in Jamaica but government is taking serious steps to address it.
propositions.quote: The Officer cited extensively from the country conditions evidence, finding that although individuals with disabilities face societal discrimination, the government of Jamaica is taking serious steps to address it.

propositions.text: Discrimination against persons with disabilities does not meet the level required by IRPA ss.96 and 97.
propositions.quote: The Officer also found that the discrimination against persons with disabilities does not rise to the level contemplated by s.96 and s.97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found discrimination against disabled persons but government efforts and no persecution level under IRPA.

propositions.text: The Officer found Applicant unlikely to be targeted due to perceived wealth from overseas employment.
propositions.quote: The Officer additionally considered country conditions evidence, and determined that the Applicant would likely not be targeted due to his perceived wealth from overseas employment.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence did not show returnees from overseas are more likely victims of crime than general population.
propositions.quote: They found that documentary evidence did not suggest that returnees from overseas are more likely to become victims of crime and violence than the general population of Jamaica.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found Applicant unlikely to be targeted for perceived wealth and no evidence returnees face more crime risk.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to rebut presumption of state protection; Jamaica is an electoral democracy with law enforcement and functioning judiciary.
propositions.quote: The Officer finally found that the Applicant had not rebutted the presumption of state protection. While acknowledging that gang-related violence and corruption remain problems in Jamaica, it is an electoral democracy with law enforcement and a functioning judiciary.

propositions.text: Serious efforts are made to reduce police corruption and adequate state protection is available to Applicant.
propositions.quote: Serious efforts are being made to reduce corruption in the police force and adequate state protection would be available to the Applicant.

propositions.text: Applicant did not provide sufficient evidence of a state policy denying protection to his target group.
propositions.quote: The Applicant did not adduce sufficient evidence to suggest that there is a broader state policy not to extend state protection to his ‘target group.’

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found Jamaica provides adequate state protection and Applicant did not rebut presumption or show state policy denying protection.

propositions.text: Officer concluded no serious possibility of persecution and insufficient evidence of personalized risk of life, torture, or cruel punishment.
propositions.quote: As a result of this analysis, the Officer concluded that there is a) no serious possibility of persecution for any reason should the Applicant be returned to Jamaica; and b) insufficient evidence to show, on a balance of probabilities, that the Applicant would face a personalized, probable risk to his life, a risk of torture, or a risk of cruel and unusual punishment in Jamaica.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer concluded no serious persecution possibility and no personalized risk of life, torture, or cruel punishment.

propositions.text: Applicant raises two issues undermining reasonableness: failure to apply operational adequacy test for state protection and misconstruing individualized risk profile.
propositions.quote: The Applicant raises two issues, both of which, he argues, undermine the reasonableness of the Officer’s decision. These are: Did the Officer fail to apply the test of operational adequacy in assessing state protection? Did the Officer misconstrue the individualized risk profile of the Applicant as a person with his disabilities?

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer failed to apply operational adequacy test and misconstrued his individualized risk profile.

propositions.text: The standard of review is reasonableness, as agreed by parties, per Vavilov 2019 SCC 65 para 23.
propositions.quote: The parties do not dispute that the standard of review is reasonableness: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 23 [Vavilov].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is reasonableness per Vavilov, agreed by parties.

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires an internally coherent, rational chain of analysis justified by facts and law (Vavilov para 85).
propositions.quote: Reasonable decisions are those that are based on an “internally coherent and rational chain of analysis that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain a decision-maker” (Vavilov at para 85).

propositions.text: Judicial review focuses on intelligibility, transparency, and justification of decision and reasons (Vavilov para 15).
propositions.quote: Judicial review of administrative action remains focused on three primary considerations in the decision-making process: intelligibility, transparency, and justification – with a focus on both the decision and the reasons for it: Vavilov at para 15.

propositions.text: These considerations must be applied with regard to individuals subject to the decision (Vavilov para 95).
propositions.quote: Moreover, Vavilov reminds us that these considerations must be considered not in the abstract, but in respect of the individuals who are subject to the administrative decision: Vavilov at para 95.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness requires coherent analysis and focuses on intelligibility, transparency, justification, respecting individuals (Vavilov).

propositions.text: PRRA stakes are profound; reasons must reflect stakes per principle of responsive justification (Vavilov para 133).
propositions.quote: The stakes associated with PRRA proceedings are profound, as they may directly implicate the life, liberty, and security of those seeking protection. Vavilov is also clear (at para 133) that, in this context, the reasons provided in support of a decision – the justification for that decision – must reflect those stakes. This is the principle of responsive justification introduced in Vavilov (at para 133).

paragraphs.summary: The court states PRRA decisions implicate life and require reasons reflecting stakes per responsive justification (Vavilov).

propositions.text: The Officer reasonably found Applicant did not rebut presumption of state protection and discrimination did not constitute personalized risk under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s Decision was reasonable. The Officer considered the documentary record and reasonably found that the Applicant had not rebutted the presumption of state protection. It was also reasonable for the Officer to conclude, based on the documentary record, that the discrimination the Applicant might face as an older person with disabilities, returning to Jamaica from overseas, did not constitute personalized risk under s.96 and s.97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer reasonably concluded Applicant failed to rebut state protection and discrimination did not constitute personalized risk.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer failed to apply correct test for state protection, focusing on Jamaican efforts rather than operational adequacy.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the Officer did not apply the correct test for assessing state protection because the decision focuses primarily on Jamaican efforts to improve protection, while the test requires consideration of the operational adequacy of such protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer wrongly focused on Jamaican efforts instead of operational adequacy in assessing state protection.

propositions.text: The Officer applied the wrong legal test by relying on Jamaican government initiatives to reduce discrimination and police corruption.
propositions.quote: The Applicant further submits that, in relying on initiatives by the Jamaican government to reduce discrimination and violence against people with disabilities, and on efforts to reduce police corruption, the Officer applied the wrong legal test, which constitutes a reviewable error.

propositions.text: The Disabilities Act of 2022 and Disabilities Rights Tribunal have not led to substantive results and do not show operational adequacy.
propositions.quote: As one example, the Applicant submits that the Disabilities Act of 2022 and the Disabilities Rights Tribunal, relied upon by the Officer, have not led to substantive results and thus do not properly demonstrate operational adequacy.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues the Officer erred by relying on Jamaican initiatives and the Disabilities Act and Tribunal which lack substantive results.

propositions.text: Disagree with Applicant that Officer's analysis was limited to efforts or that Officer erred in applying operational adequacy test.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with the Applicant that the Officer’s analysis was limited to efforts, or that the Officer erred in failing to apply the operational adequacy test.

paragraphs.summary: Court disagrees that Officer limited analysis to efforts or erred on operational adequacy test.

propositions.text: Officer discussed Jamaican government efforts to improve disability rights, which alone does not establish error.
propositions.quote: It is true that the Officer discussed the efforts of the Jamaican government to improve rights protection for people with disabilities. But this, in itself, does not establish an error.

propositions.text: Efforts are a precursor to effective operational change and relevant for decision-makers to discuss.
propositions.quote: Efforts are generally a precursor to effective operational change. To this extent, while not in itself sufficient, it is often relevant for a decision-maker to discuss state efforts.

propositions.text: Officer's analysis went beyond efforts by considering the effect of those efforts, so no failure to apply operational adequacy standard.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s analysis of state efforts does not, on its own, indicate a failure to properly apply the operational adequacy standard, and I find that the Officer did go further in their analysis by also considering the effect of those efforts.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer discussed efforts appropriately and considered their effect, applying operational adequacy standard properly.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably found Applicant failed to rebut presumption of state protection due to insufficient documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: Further, it was reasonable for the Officer to determine that the Applicant had not provided sufficient documentary evidence to rebut the presumption of state protection.

propositions.text: Officer cited evidence that Jamaica made significant strides implementing policies promoting rights of persons with disabilities, including Disabilities Act 2022.
propositions.quote: For example, the Officer cited documentary evidence establishing that Jamaica has made “significant strides” in implementing several policies to promote the rights of persons with disabilities, including the Disabilities Act of February 2022.

propositions.text: Disabilities Act incorporated codes of practice on education, employment, health care, and created Disabilities Rights Tribunal to hear breaches.
propositions.quote: The Act incorporated codes of practices addressing education and training; employment, health care and health facilities; and brought into existence the Disabilities Rights Tribunal to hear and settle breaches of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Officer reasonably found Applicant failed to rebut state protection presumption, citing Jamaica's policy strides including Disabilities Act and Tribunal.

propositions.text: Disabilities Rights Tribunal is not yet active, questioning Officer's operational adequacy assessment.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that the same documentary evidence suggests that the Disabilities Rights Tribunal is not yet active, calling into question whether the Officer assessed the application through the prism of operational adequacy.

propositions.text: Disagree; Tribunal inactivity was reasonably explained by Officer as due to no complaints received, a reasonable finding.
propositions.quote: I disagree with this argument for two reasons: first, the argument related to the Tribunal was put to the PRRA officer, who reasonably rejected it, noting that the reason it was not active was simply that it had not yet received any complaints.

propositions.text: Applicant may disagree but Officer's finding on Tribunal inactivity was reasonably open based on documentary record.
propositions.quote: The Applicant may disagree with this finding, but it was reasonably open to the Officer, based on the documentary record.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Tribunal inactivity undermines operational adequacy; court finds Officer reasonably explained inactivity due to no complaints.

propositions.text: Applicant's argument seeks to reverse the onus of the state protection test.
propositions.quote: Second, the Applicant’s argument essentially seeks to reverse the onus of the state protection test: Camargo v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 1044; Magonza v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 14; Rstic v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 249; Galamb v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1230; Cervenakova v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 477; Majlat v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 965.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's argument improperly seeks to reverse the burden of proof in state protection test.

propositions.text: Applicant bears burden to prove Jamaican state efforts would be ineffective in his case.
propositions.quote: The Applicant bore the burden of establishing that the Jamaican state efforts to protect persons with disabilities would not be effective in his case.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably concluded Applicant did not discharge burden; analysis was rational, reasons intelligible and justified.
propositions.quote: I find that the Officer reasonably concluded that the Applicant had not discharged this burden. There was a rational chain of analysis connecting the evidence to the Officer’s conclusions and the Officer’s reasons were intelligible, transparent and adequately justified.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicant bore burden and Officer reasonably concluded burden not met with rational, justified reasons.

propositions.text: Officer properly considered operational adequacy by noting both improvements and shortcomings in Jamaican disability rights regime.
propositions.quote: Third, when read globally and in context, it is clear that the Officer properly considered the issue of operational adequacy, noting both the improvements and shortcomings in the Jamaican disability rights regime.

propositions.text: Acknowledging shortcomings in state protection efforts may show operational adequacy test was applied through balanced evidence assessment.
propositions.quote: This Court has held that acknowledging the shortcomings in a government’s state protection efforts may indicate that an officer considered and applied the operational adequacy test through a balanced assessment of the evidence: see Go v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1021 at para 13; and De Lourdes Gonzalez Duran v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 855 at para 17.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer balanced improvements and shortcomings, applying operational adequacy test properly, supported by precedent.

propositions.text: Officer noted Jamaica has mechanisms to address discrimination and laws prohibiting disability discrimination but acknowledged incomplete implementation and lack of accessibility mandates.
propositions.quote: The Officer noted that Jamaica has mechanisms in place to investigate and address incidents of discrimination against persons with disabilities; and that Jamaican law prohibits discrimination on the basis of disability, but also acknowledged that the law has not been fully implemented and does not mandate accessibility standards.

propositions.text: Overall, Officer's evidentiary assessment was balanced and reasonable.
propositions.quote: On the whole, I find the Officer’s assessment of the evidentiary record to be balanced and reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Officer acknowledged Jamaica's anti-discrimination laws and shortcomings; overall assessment was balanced and reasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant submits Officer erred by failing to properly consider his risk profile as older person with disabilities and returnee to Jamaica.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the Officer made another reviewable error in failing to properly consider his risk profile as an older person with disabilities and a returnee to Jamaica from overseas.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer failed to properly consider his risk profile as older disabled returnee to Jamaica.

propositions.text: Officer considered Applicant's full risk profile and reasonably found no substantial risk beyond general Jamaican population.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Officer considered the Applicant’s full risk profile and reasonably determined that his personal circumstances did not subject him to a risk substantially different from the general Jamaican population.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably concluded discrimination would not reach level described in IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: The Respondent further argues that the Officer reasonably concluded that while the Applicant might experience some discrimination in Jamaica, he had not established that it would rise to the level of treatment as described in sections 96 and 97 of the 1RPA.

propositions.text: Applicant's arguments amount to reweighing evidence, which Court should reject.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Applicant’s arguments simply amount to asking this Court to reweigh the evidence. I agree.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Officer reasonably assessed risk and discrimination level; Applicant just asks Court to reweigh evidence, which is rejected.

propositions.text: Officers must assess risk cumulatively and intersectionally based on Applicant's whole profile, supported by multiple cases.
propositions.quote: It is well established that Officers are generally required to assess risk cumulatively, and intersectionally, on the basis of an Applicant’s whole profile: see for example Virk v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 399 at paras 36-39; Rodriguez Ramos v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 41 at para 21; Kundukhashvili v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1081 at para 50-52; Magoya v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 516 at para 37; Go v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1021 at paras 22-23; Djubok v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 497 at paras 18-25.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites precedent that Officers must assess risk cumulatively and intersectionally based on whole profile.

propositions.text: Officer considered Applicant's disability and returnee status as principal risk factors and reasonably concluded insufficient evidence of mistreatment under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: In this case, I find that the Officer appreciated the key aspects of the Applicant’s profile, and undertook the risk assessment on this basis. The Officer considered the Applicant’s risk as a person with disabilities. The Officer additionally assessed the Applicant’s risk as someone who would return to Jamaica after a prolonged period of absence from the country. These were the principal bases on which the Applicant asserted a risk of harm. When read globally, I find that the Officer adequately considered these risk factors, and reasonably concluded that the Applicant had adduced insufficient evidence to demonstrate that his personal circumstances would attract the kind of mistreatment contemplated by sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer adequately considered Applicant's disability and returnee risk factors and reasonably found insufficient evidence of mistreatment.

propositions.text: Courts must show deference to decision-maker's core factual findings.
propositions.quote: It is trite law that courts are to exhibit deference in reviewing a decision-maker’s core findings of fact.

propositions.text: Officer adequately evaluated country conditions and found Applicant would not face harm attracting IRPA protection.
propositions.quote: Here, the Officer adequately evaluated and referred to the country conditions evidence in determining that the Applicant would not face the kinds of harm, upon return to Jamaica that attract protection under sections 96 or 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Court states deference to factual findings and finds Officer adequately evaluated country conditions and risk of harm.

propositions.text: Dismiss application for judicial review; no reviewable errors warrant intervention despite sympathy for Applicant.
propositions.quote: For the above reasons, I dismiss this application for judicial review. While I have the utmost sympathy for the Applicant’s situation, I have concluded that the underlying decision in this matter contains no reviewable errors that warrant the intervention of this Court.

propositions.text: Applicant's compelling circumstances should be considered in pending humanitarian and compassionate permanent residence application.
propositions.quote: This does not detract from the compelling circumstances of Mr. Smith’s case, which I trust will be considered in his pending application for permanent residence in Canada on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review, finds no errors, but acknowledges Applicant's compelling circumstances for other application.

propositions.text: No question for certification arises; judicial review application dismissed.
propositions.quote: The parties did not propose a question for certification in this matter, and I agree that none arises. JUDGMENT in IMM-488-23 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question is certified for appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review and certifies no question for appeal.
